evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with acute kidney injury in the emergency department and acute wards, including emergency hyperkalaemia. Verified against KDIGO 2012, NICE NG148 (updated 2024) and the UK Kidney Association hyperkalaemia guideline (2023). Note: KDIGO published an updated AKI guideline in 2026 that was not accessible for this check.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: KDIGO 2026 AKI guideline update not reviewed
Availability of potassium binders on the hospital formulary

pathophysiology.summary: AKI is an abrupt fall in kidney function measured by a rise in serum creatinine and/or a fall in urine output. Causes are pre-renal (reduced perfusion), intrinsic renal (tubular, interstitial, glomerular or vascular injury) and post-renal (urinary tract obstruction); several often coexist.
keyMechanisms: Pre-renal: hypovolaemia, sepsis, heart failure, liver disease and drugs that reduce glomerular perfusion (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, diuretics) lower GFR; prolonged hypoperfusion progresses to ischaemic tubular injury.

Intrinsic: acute tubular injury (sepsis, ischaemia, nephrotoxins such as aminoglycosides and iodinated contrast), acute interstitial nephritis, glomerulonephritis or vasculitis (haematuria + proteinuria), myeloma.
Post-renal: obstruction (stones, prostate, tumour) raises tubular pressure; bilateral obstruction, obstruction of a solitary kidney or infected obstruction (pyonephrosis) is an emergency.

Consequences: reduced excretion of potassium, acid and water causes hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, fluid overload and pulmonary oedema; retained uraemic toxins cause pericarditis and encephalopathy.
Creatinine lags behind the fall in GFR, so early AKI may show only oliguria.

symptoms: Often none — detected on blood tests.
Reduced urine output; symptoms of the cause (vomiting, diarrhoea, sepsis, urinary symptoms).
physicalSigns: Volume status: hypovolaemia (tachycardia, hypotension, dry mucosa) or overload (raised JVP, crackles, oedema).
Purpuric rash, arthritis or haemoptysis (vasculitis — multi-system disease).
redFlags: Potassium 6.5 mmol/L or more, or ECG changes of hyperkalaemia
Pulmonary oedema or fluid overload not responding to treatment
Suspected pyonephrosis (infected obstructed kidney) or obstructed solitary kidney
precipitants: Nephrotoxic drugs in the past week: NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics; iodinated contrast.
Risk factors: CKD (eGFR below 60), heart failure, liver disease, diabetes, previous AKI, age 65 or over.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Known low eGFR, small kidneys, anaemia; but a rise in creatinine in CKD may still be AKI (NICE 1.1.3).
Haemolysed sample or delayed processing; repeat from a large vein with prompt analysis.
High muscle mass, creatine supplements, some drugs (trimethoprim) — interpret against baseline.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: At presentation; compare with baseline; then daily in hospital
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Rise of 26 µmol/L or more within 48 h, or 1.5× baseline or more within 7 days.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Stage 1: 1.5–1.9× baseline or rise of 26.5 µmol/L or more. Stage 2: 2.0–2.9×. Stage 3: 3.0× or more, or creatinine 353.6 µmol/L or more, or RRT started.
ruleIn.normalValue: Creatinine about 60–110 µmol/L (varies with muscle mass); compare with the patient's baseline

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Within 6 h if pyonephrosis is suspected; within 24 h if no cause is identified or obstruction is possible. Not routine when the cause is known

references.title: NICE NG148: Acute kidney injury: prevention, detection and management

clinicalManagement.title: Detect, stage and look for life-threatening complications
actions: Confirm AKI by creatinine rise or oliguria; stage with KDIGO; compare with baseline.
Check potassium, acid–base, fluid status and ECG straight away.
Urine dipstick and record the likely cause in the notes.

clinicalManagement.title: Treat hyperkalaemia (5-step approach)
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately if K+ 6.5 or more or ECG changes
actions: STEP 1 Protect the heart if ECG changes: 30 mL 10% calcium gluconate IV over 10 min (calcium chloride 10 mL 10% over 5 min in cardiac arrest/peri-arrest). Repeat if ECG changes persist.

STEP 2 Shift K+ into cells: soluble insulin 10 units in 25 g glucose IV (severe; suggested for moderate). If pre-treatment glucose below 7.0 mmol/L, follow with 10% glucose 50 mL/h for 5 h. Add nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg (never alone). No routine IV sodium bicarbonate.
STEP 3 Remove K+: sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g three times daily for up to 72 h (severe; consider for moderate), or patiromer 8.4 g once daily. Calcium resonium no longer routine.
STEP 4 Monitor: K+ at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 h; glucose at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, 300 and 360 min after insulin.
STEP 5 Prevent recurrence: stop potassium supplements and drugs that raise potassium; renal or critical care referral if severe or refractory.

clinicalManagement.title: Restore perfusion
actions: Hypovolaemia: isotonic crystalloid rather than colloid (albumin or starches) (KDIGO 3.1.1).
Shock: vasopressors together with fluids (KDIGO 3.1.2); protocol-based haemodynamic management in septic shock.
Fluid overloaded: no further fluid; loop diuretic only for overload while awaiting RRT or during recovery.

clinicalManagement.title: Stop and adjust drugs
actions: Temporarily stop ACE inhibitors and ARBs (with diarrhoea, vomiting or sepsis), NSAIDs, diuretics and other nephrotoxins; avoid aminoglycosides if alternatives exist.
Pharmacist review of all doses for current kidney function.
Do not use loop diuretics to treat AKI itself, or low-dose dopamine (KDIGO 3.4.2, 3.5.1; NICE 1.5.3, 1.5.5).
Do not delay iodinated contrast in an emergency when delay is clinically significant (NICE 1.1.7).

clinicalManagement.title: Find and treat the cause
actions: Obstruction: catheter for bladder outflow; urology referral; nephrostomy or stent within 12 h; immediate referral if pyonephrosis, solitary kidney, bilateral obstruction or complications.
Nephrology within 24 h if: possible vasculitis, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis or myeloma; no clear cause; poor response; complications; stage 3; transplant; or CKD stage 4–5.

clinicalManagement.title: Renal replacement therapy
actions: Refer immediately when not responding to medical treatment: hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, uraemic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy), fluid overload or pulmonary oedema (NICE 1.5.8).
Decide on the whole clinical picture and trends, not an isolated urea, creatinine or potassium (KDIGO 5.1.2; NICE 1.5.9).
Airway, breathing, circulation or conscious-level problems: critical care team first (UKKA 19.4).

keyPoints: AKI = creatinine up 26 µmol/L in 48 h, 1.5× in 7 days, or urine below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h.
Check potassium, ECG and acid–base first.
Calcium protects the heart; insulin–glucose and salbutamol shift potassium; binders or dialysis remove it.
Stop nephrotoxins and ACE inhibitors/ARBs; dose-adjust all drugs.
Dipstick everyone; ultrasound if cause unclear or obstruction possible.
pitfalls: Treating a haemolysed potassium without repeating — or delaying treatment of a real one.
Insulin–glucose without glucose monitoring for 6 h.
Furosemide to 'make urine' in oliguric AKI.
Missing obstruction or vasculitis (blood + protein on dipstick).

patientEducation: Avoid over-the-counter NSAIDs; stay hydrated during vomiting or diarrhoea.
Sick-day guidance: which medicines to pause when unwell.
lifestyleAndDiet: Not applicable in the acute phase.
mdtReferrals: Nephrology (criteria above); urology for obstruction; critical care for unstable or RRT-requiring patients.
dischargeCriteria: Creatinine falling towards baseline and potassium stable without ongoing treatment.
Cause identified and treated; euvolaemic; drug changes documented.
Plan for which stopped medicines to restart, and when.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Monitor creatinine after discharge (frequency by stability); review at 3 months for resolution or new/worse CKD (KDIGO 2.3.4); nephrology if eGFR 30 or less after recovery (NICE 1.5.16).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Creatinine rise 26.5 µmol/L or more within 48 h; OR 1.5× baseline or more within 7 days; OR urine below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h
1.5–1.9× baseline or rise of 26.5 µmol/L or more; urine below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 h
2.0–2.9× baseline; urine below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 12 h or more
3.0× baseline, or creatinine 353.6 µmol/L or more, or RRT started; urine below 0.3 mL/kg/h for 24 h or more, or anuria 12 h or more
Mild 5.5–5.9; moderate 6.0–6.4; severe 6.5 mmol/L or more

adjustments: Calcium chloride 10% 10 mL over 5 min in cardiac arrest or peri-arrest
If pre-treatment glucose below 7.0 mmol/L: 10% glucose 50 mL/h for 5 h afterwards
Never as monotherapy in severe hyperkalaemia

medicationPlan.note: Doses as stated in the UK Kidney Association 2023 guideline. Check SFDA registration and hospital formulary — sodium zirconium cyclosilicate and patiromer may not be on every Saudi formulary; follow the local hyperkalaemia protocol where they are unavailable.

guidelineComparison.title: KDIGO 2012 vs NICE NG148 — where they differ

values: IV isotonic saline or bicarbonate for at-risk patients; not oral fluids alone; oral NAC suggested
Encourage oral hydration; IV volume expansion only for particularly high-risk inpatients (e.g. eGFR below 30)
Not specified as a timed standard
Within 6 h if pyonephrosis suspected; within 24 h if no cause or obstruction risk; not routine if cause known
Within 24 h for stage 3, unclear cause, suspected intrinsic disease, transplant or CKD 4–5

guidelineComparison.note: Both agree: crystalloids not colloids, no diuretics or dopamine to treat AKI, and start RRT on the whole clinical picture rather than one number.
